title: AI exposure: what the company itself is willing to tell the SEC
what: The natural worry about a firm whose product is expert brainpower is that AI does the work more cheaply. This chart counts how often Exponent discusses AI in each annual report, and marks the year it first added a formal risk factor warning that AI may REDUCE demand for its services. The panel underneath quotes that risk factor in full, alongside the sentence where the company scopes what it thinks is actually at risk.
how: We read the last six Exponent 10-K annual reports straight from SEC EDGAR and counted mentions of 'AI', 'artificial intelligence' and 'machine learning', then searched for the risk-factor heading about AI reducing demand. Everything quoted is lifted verbatim. Nothing is scored: there is no model here, only counts of words in filings and the passages themselves. The final box compares that against our own court data, where each Exponent expert had to appear in person.
thesis: This cuts both ways and is presented that way. Bear: mentions jumped roughly eight-fold in the FY2025 report and the demand-reduction risk factor is BRAND NEW - management now considers AI substitution real enough to disclose to regulators, which is a genuine change to the story. Bull: the company's own scoping sentence puts the exposure on offerings 'more standardized in nature', which is the opposite of a bespoke failure investigation defended under cross-examination; and roughly 60% of revenue is reactive work where Rule 702 requires a human expert who can be deposed. A model cannot be sworn in, impeached, or sued for malpractice.
caveats: This does NOT measure whether AI can do Exponent's work. No public dataset answers that honestly, and inventing a score would be exactly the kind of number this project refuses to print.
Counting mentions measures ATTENTION, not danger. Risk factors are written defensively by lawyers to disclose what could go wrong - adding one is not a prediction that it will.

The word count includes AI as an OPPORTUNITY. Exponent sells AI and machine-learning consulting through its own Data Sciences practice, and some mentions concern its internal use of AI tools. Read the quoted passages rather than the bar height.

Management's framing of where the risk sits is self-interested. It is quoted because it is a specific, checkable claim they chose to make to the SEC under legal exposure - not because they are disinterested.

The courtroom-bench share is a LOWER BOUND, built only from practices we could tie to a named testifying expert in the federal opinions we sampled. Consulting experts never appear in court records and state courts are sparsely covered, so the true testimony-anchored share is higher.
